“Did you get a bag?” Avery asked.

“Yes.”

“Do you have the leash?”

“Yeah.”

“Just get ou-“

“We’re going.”

We walked through the neighborhood’s parked Smart cars, Japanese maples, smiling faces cooking dinner seen through the bay windows. We reached the top of the hill in the park and came back through an alley lined with streetlights, though I had never seen anyone else walk through. At the end of it I tossed Ci’s droppings, wrapped in a bag, into a neighbor’s garbage.

“This your house?”

A short-statured man walked out from behind a rusted-out car, dressed like he came off the Appalachian trail; light fleece, pants made of breathable mesh, hiking boots, light scruff, beady eyes.

“No, I live over on Ferrison. Well, my girlfriend does.”

“So this isn’t your garbage can, correct?”

“No.”

“So, you put your dog’s shit in someone else’s garbage can?”

“Technically, she’s not my dog. She’s my girlfriend’s dog. Well, my girlfriend doesn’t really believe in ‘owning’ a dog, so… she’s like her own dog.”

He took a step forward under the streetlight.

“Please remove your dog’s shit from this garbage can.”

“Is this your garbage can?”

“No. But it’s not yours either. Please, I’m asking again, just get it out.”

“Listen, man, it’s just – “

I woke up to CI sniffing the bag, placed on my chest, and somebody shaking me and asking if I was there. My left eye was puffy and hard to see out of. From the corner of my right eye I saw her kneel down and take the bag off me and put it in the garbage.

“I was worried; you were gone for more than 20 minutes so I came out to find you and Ci and here you are.”

She took us inside and I fell asleep with the light on while she brushed her teeth and Ci chewed on a stuffed bear of hers.
